title: What the system holds and where its capacity comes from
subtitle: A way of reading infrastructure that shows what is yours and what is borrowed
whyItMatters: Two systems serving the same load can be in completely different states, and that difference only appears once you separate the capacity you own from the capacity you are borrowing.
openingQuestion: Two systems each handle 10,000 requests per second. Which one is more durable?
openingOptions: The one leaning less on capacity that expands with demand, because that kind can be absent at the moment it is needed most
The one with more machines, since the load is spread thinner and each machine carries less
The one with lower infrastructure cost, because it is using its resources more efficiently
They are equivalent, since both serve the same amount of load
explanation: Capacity that scales with demand is very convenient and it is borrowed: it depends on the vendor still having free machines, on your account limits, and on you still being able to pay. All three can fall short at once, and they fall short exactly when demand rises sharply - which is when they are needed.

See what the borrowed part depends on
Know which shock the system survives

realWorldExample.company: An account limit, not a shortage of machines
realWorldExample.description: A system was designed to add machines as load rose, had been tested repeatedly, and always worked. During a real peak the machine count stopped at thirty and went no further. The vendor had not run out - the account carried a default limit of thirty for that type, set the day it was opened, and because nobody had ever reached it nobody knew it existed.

sections.text: The reading below borrows its shape from a reconciliation, and it is useful for the same reason: it forces two sides to agree, so anything that does not agree is something being left out.

variables.name: All the capacity the system genuinely uses
variables.description: Measured in units of work: requests per second, records per minute, or terabytes stored.

variables.name: The share running on resources reserved and paid for in advance
variables.description: Always present, dependent on nobody, and its limit is a number known ahead of time.

variables.name: The share resting on elastic capacity or an external service
variables.description: Cheap when there is slack and capable of being absent when needed. This is the side to read carefully.

variables.name: The gap between capacity held and load on the busiest day
variables.description: Negative means the system is living on the busiest day not having arrived yet. Many systems are in this state without knowing.

sections.text: Three questions for the borrowed side

items: What does this share depend on, and has that party committed to anything in writing
Is any limit capping it from above, including one nobody has ever reached
If the borrowed share vanished entirely, what percentage could the system still serve

sections.text: The third is the most worth asking and the least often asked, because it turns a vague worry into a number. A system that still serves seventy percent with the borrowed part gone is in a completely different position from one that serves five, even though both run well today.

sections.label: A quota is the worst kind of limit
sections.text: A server running out of capacity means the system slows down and there is time to react. An account quota does not slow down - it blocks flatly at a number, usually a default nobody chose, and it only reveals itself the first time you reach it. A list of every quota applying to your system is a cheap document to produce and almost no team has one.
Read it over time, not once

The ratio between the owned and borrowed shares tends to drift one way: every time capacity is needed urgently, borrowing more is the fastest route. No single decision in that chain is wrong, and after two years the system depends on the borrowed share at a level nobody ever considered.

sections.title: If the borrowed part disappears, how much can we still serve
sections.task: Four capacity sources, in requests per second (illustrative numbers). A source with a quota can only be used up to the quota even if you rent more. Compute the capacity really usable, the part blocked by quotas, and the percentage still served when all borrowed sources are lost. The starter adds the capacity directly and ignores quotas.
hints: For each source, the usable part is min(capacity, quota) when a quota exists.
The final percentage divides the owned part by the usable capacity, not by the nominal capacity.

sections.title: Owned, borrowed and quota: a story about housing
sections.intro: Think about where a family lives. Some rooms are bought outright, some are rented by the day, and there are limits nobody notices until they hit them.
rows: A house already bought, always available
How many rooms? The limit is a number known in advance
Renting a room by the day or staying with an acquaintance
What does the agreement say, and if they stop letting you stay, how much space is left
A lift marked for eight people at most, which nobody knows about because nine have never stood in it
Which limit applies that nobody has ever reached
sections.oneLiner: Ask the system what percentage it can still serve when every borrowed part is gone, then list the quotas nobody has touched.

s.text: The system serves 4000 requests per second at peak: 1500 on machines the team owns, 2500 on rented elastic capacity. The boss asks: are we safe? What do you ask first?

choices.label: Is the system slow today, and if not then we count as safe
If the rented part disappeared, how much could the system still serve
How many percent cheaper per month the rented part is than the owned part

a.text: It is not slow today because nobody has touched the quota. Next week a surge hits the default account quota, and the system is not slowed gradually but cut off flatly.

c.text: Cost is a fair question but not the safety question. You have a nice price comparison and still do not know what remains if the borrowed part is gone.

b.text: 1500 out of 4000 means about 38% remains when the borrowed part is gone. That turns a vague worry into a number. You also notice the account quota is at its default. What do you do?

choices.label: List every quota, raise those near the peak, add alerts
Buy enough owned machines for 4000 requests immediately

d.text: A quota is the worst kind of limit because it cuts off flatly at a default number. With quotas raised and alerts in place, the biggest risk is covered at small cost.

e.text: Buying for 4000 gives up the benefit of elasticity, and you still do not know which quota is waiting to be hit. You pay a lot for half an answer.

lines: The same amount of load does not mean the same condition.
A quota blocks flatly, and it only shows itself the first time you reach it.

quiz.question: Why is elastic capacity considered borrowed?
options: Because the vendor may reclaim this class of resource before reclaiming what is prepaid
Because it is billed by the hour, so the monthly total is hard to predict in advance
Because it takes time to start up, so it cannot respond fast enough to sudden surges
Because it rests on conditions that tend to fall short at exactly the moment it is needed most, since those conditions share a common cause
quiz.explanation: The other three are true and all are disadvantages. The core point is simultaneity: the vendor running out, your quota hitting its ceiling, and demand surging all tend to happen together, because they have a common cause.

quiz.question: Which question turns worry about the borrowed share into a number?
options: If the borrowed share vanished, what percentage could the system still serve
What share of monthly infrastructure cost does the borrowed part represent
What availability has the vendor committed to for this class of elastic resource
How long would it take to move the borrowed share onto reserved capacity
quiz.explanation: The other three yield numbers too and all measure something else. The first measures the thing you need to know - how bad the worst case is - and it usually returns a figure far lower than the team's intuition.

quiz.question: Why is a quota more dangerous than a server running out of capacity?
options: Because raising a quota goes through the vendor, which takes several working days
Because it blocks flatly instead of slowing down, so the team gets no time at all to notice and improvise
Because quotas apply at the account level, so they affect every system at once
Because monitoring tools usually do not track usage against quota limits
quiz.explanation: The other three make it worse. The first is the root cause: a system that slows down gives the team a few minutes, and a hard wall gives them none.

quiz.question: Why does the borrowed share tend to grow over time?
options: Because new services are usually designed to run on elastic capacity from the start
Because the price of elastic resources falls over time, making it steadily more attractive
Because every time capacity is needed urgently, borrowing more is the fastest route available
Because reserved capacity contracts expire and are not always renewed when they do
quiz.explanation: This is the shape of every technical debt: each decision was reasonable at the time, none of them deserves objection, and their sum is a state nobody ever chose.

quiz.question: What does a negative capacity buffer mean?
options: The capacity measurement is faulty, since a gap cannot hold a negative value
The system is consuming more resources than the budget approved for it
The system needs more machines immediately, because current load already exceeds what it serves
The system is living on the busiest day not having arrived yet
quiz.explanation: A negative buffer does not mean the system is failing today - today's load may be well below its busiest. It means there is no reserve left for the busiest day, and that day arrives without warning.

keyTakeaways: The same amount of load does not mean the same condition
The borrowed share rests on conditions that tend to fall short together
A quota blocks flatly and only shows itself the first time you reach it
The borrowed ratio drifts upward with no single decision being wrong

practicePrompt.question: A system serves 10,000 requests per second: 3,000 reserved and 7,000 elastic. Losing all the elastic leaves what share?
options: 70% (= taking the elastic share rather than the reserved share that remains)
100% (= assuming reserved capacity automatically absorbs the missing load)
0% (= assuming losing the elastic share stops the whole system serving)
practicePrompt.explanation: 3,000 out of 10,000 is 30%. That figure is worth writing down because it says seven users in ten go unserved in the bad case, while every chart today is green.

summary.keyIdea: Separate owned capacity from borrowed before judging what a system can take
summary.commonMistake: Reading a total capacity figure without asking which share is borrowed
summary.action: List every quota applying to the system you look after, including untouched ones.

application.title: Three numbers for the system you hold
application.message: How much is owned. How much is borrowed. What share could still be served if the borrowed part disappeared.
application.secondary: The third is usually far lower than the whole team's intuition, and that is why it is worth writing down.
